analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting older workers' pension and benefit packages because of age.
analysis.headline: Sens. Hatch and Kassebaum's bill to protect older workers' benefits was referred to a Senate Labor subcommittee on Aug. 7, 1990 and never received a committee or floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Age Discrimination in Employment Act to make it illegal to reduce or deny a worker's pension, health, disability, or severance benefits because of age. It came in response to a 1989 Supreme Court decision that had limited age-discrimination protection for benefits. But it also wrote broad exceptions into law: employers could make age-based benefit distinctions that pass an equal-cost or actuarial-value test or serve a "legitimate business purpose," and union contracts got up to two extra years before having to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Older workers would have gained a federal discrimination claim if an employer reduced their pension, health, disability, or severance benefits because of their age, unless the employer met one of the bill's safe harbors. Employers also stood to gain: after the Supreme Court's Betts decision left the law unsettled, the bill spelled out exactly which long-standing benefit designs — coordinated pensions, Social Security offsets, early retirement subsidies — would be lawful going forward.

how_it_helps.text: Made it unlawful to discriminate against any worker in employee benefits because of age, restoring protection that the Supreme Court's 1989 Betts decision had placed in doubt.

Covered the full range of compensation — pensions, health insurance, disability, severance, supplemental unemployment benefits, and coordination with Social Security and workers' compensation — rather than leaving older workers to challenge each type separately.
Expressly protected enhanced early retirement offers, so employers could keep subsidizing early retirement for older subgroups of employees without those offers counting as discrimination.

Gave employers a clear compliance roadmap: the bill defined lawful arrangements (equal cost, equal present value, or an option to take the younger workers' benefit), required the EEOC to consult Labor and Treasury before issuing rules, and delayed coverage of collective bargaining agreements for up to 24 months so plans had time to adjust.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would have borne the cost: redesigning benefit arrangements, paying for actuarial determinations to prove equal cost or present value, and defending "legitimate business purpose" justifications in EEOC complaints and lawsuits. The EEOC, Labor Department, and Treasury would have taken on new rulemaking and enforcement duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with pension and benefit plans

drawbacks.text: The exceptions were broad. An employer could still make any age-based difference in benefits by asserting a "legitimate business purpose," and could hand older workers smaller actual benefits as long as the annual cost or actuarial present value equaled what younger workers received.
Enforcement would have hinged on complex actuarial "present value" calculations, which favor employers with the resources to litigate them over individual workers trying to prove a benefit gap.

Many older workers would have waited years for protection: union contracts were grandfathered until expiration or 24 months (whichever came first), state disability plans only had to change for new hires, and benefit payment series already underway when the law took effect were exempted entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Older workers would have gained a federal remedy for benefit discrimination for the first time since the Betts decision, which is a real gain. But the bill was written as much to reassure employers as to protect workers: the "legitimate business purpose" exception and the equal-cost/present-value tests would have allowed plenty of age-based benefit differences to continue lawfully, and the grandfathering meant many workers would have seen no change for years. As drafted, the protection was genuine but leaky, and proving a violation would have required actuarial evidence most individual workers cannot easily produce.

outcome.mechanism: It died quietly: two months after introduction it was sent to a Senate Labor subcommittee that never acted on it, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Supreme Court's 1989 Betts decision held that the Age Discrimination in Employment Act had limited application to employee benefits, leaving employers and older workers uncertain about when age-based benefit differences were lawful.
Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the Employee Benefits Equity Act on July 10, 1990, joined by Sen. Nancy Kassebaum; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
On August 7, 1990, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor, where the record shows no further action of any kind.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still sitting in subcommittee — no committee markup, no floor vote, no roll call ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead in the immediate sense: with the bill dead, the post-Betts gap in which age-based benefit differences were difficult to challenge continued, and no employer had to operate under the bill's liability rules. Older workers were not left without recourse for long, though — Congress passed the stricter Older Workers Benefit Protection Act later in 1990, which set a tougher equal-benefit standard than this bill and did not include its broad 'legitimate business purpose' exception.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers briefly; workers got a stricter law instead

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 10, 1990 to extend Age Discrimination in Employment Act protections to employee benefits while carving out safe harbors for existing benefit designs.

for.name: Nancy Kassebaum
for.what_they_did: Joined Hatch in introducing the bill at its introduction.

against.name: Senate Subcommittee on Labor
against.role: Subcommittee, Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on August 7, 1990 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Edward M. Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee for a markup or vote after its July 1990 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so partisan alignment was never tested: the sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans (2 of 45 Senate Republicans), while the bill died without action in the Democratic-controlled Senate Labor Committee.

industries.industry: Employers offering pensions and health benefits
industries.note: The bill would have created new age-discrimination liability for benefit plan design, but it also codified employer safe harbors: equal-cost and equal-present-value tests, 'legitimate business purpose' variances, and a grace period before coverage took effect. The employer interest in maximum flexibility to tailor benefits by age runs directly against older workers' interest in equal treatment.

Collective bargaining agreements were grandfathered until expiration or 24 months, whichever came first, giving union plans time to adjust but delaying protection for older union members covered by existing contracts.
